items.finding: Low-level data fusion is described as the simplest combination approach, where variables from different sources are concatenated into a single new data matrix.
items.how_it_applies: This supports the planned low-level fusion design (one PLS model per method, then joining synchronised spectra into one augmented matrix) as a recognised, simple fusion architecture worth testing in the pilot.
items.limits_and_transfer_risks: The review is general PAT literature, not cell culture spectroscopy; it does not address block scaling, time synchronisation, or bioreactor probe placement, so those design details remain unvalidated for this process.

citation.quote: Low-level data fusion (LLDF) is considered the simplest method to achieve a combination of inputs. In this case, the data is rearranged into a new data matrix, where the variables coming from different sources are placed one after the other.
citation.label: E01 ¶31

items.finding: The review states that the contribution and complementarity of each dataset should be evaluated before fusing data from multiple sources.
items.how_it_applies: This aligns with the acceptance rule that the fused model must beat the better single method on held-out runs; the assessment should include a per-method contribution check before committing to the second instrument.
items.limits_and_transfer_risks: The statement is a general recommendation without quantitative criteria or application domain, so it does not define how much improvement is required or how it behaves with drifting, changing cell culture media.

citation.quote: Before fusing data from multiple sources, it is essential to evaluate the contribution of each dataset to the model and its complementarity.
citation.label: E01 ¶82

items.finding: A cited Raman and FT-IR food study showed that instrument complementarity alone was sometimes not sufficient to improve prediction of several quality attributes.
items.how_it_applies: This is a reason to treat the second instrument as conditional: the pilot should verify on held-out runs that fusion actually improves glucose/lactate prediction before keeping both probes.
items.limits_and_transfer_risks: The finding comes from a food analytical study, not an aqueous cell culture process, and concerns different analytes and matrices, so the outcome may differ here.

citation.quote: In some situations, instrument complementarity (not data complementarity) was not sufficient to improve the performance of predictive several CQAs, as shown by a Raman and FT-IR data based food analytical study [73].
citation.label: E01 ¶36
